newsitem.title: USA: Performance is business computing priority-study.
newsitem.headline: Performance is business computing priority-study.

text.p: After years of cutbacks, corporate computing executives are placing performance and prospects for creating revenues ahead of cost cutting as their top priorities, a study said.

The study, to be released on Monday, prepared by Find/SVP's Strategic Research Division, also found that a high percentage of respondents were concerned about creating high volumes of data that were not being properly managed.
Some 93 percent of those surveyed in the United States were concerned about performance and response time, up 9 percent from a year ago, while concern over data security has fallen to 86 percent.

Greater concern over performance comes as many companies are incorporating Internet technologies into their computing environments, and some using public networks fear congestion will turn the World Wide Web into the "World Wide Wait".

In a sign managers of data centres expect to gain a central role in the growth of distributed computing, executives project 35 percent growth over the next two years in the number of servers under their control.

Janice Porell, vice president of strategic marketing at EMC Corp., which commissioned the study, said it was a sign that downsizing as a trend, especially in the United States, now appears to be losing momentum.

"It looks to us like information is becoming more critical to the organisation," she said in an interview, adding that rather than simply being viewed as a cost, this trend "supports the notion of providing a competitive edge."
Large-scale organisations are thus looking to information officers to play far more of an entrepreneurial role, using information processing to provide market leadership.
"Once you're ahead, everyone else is in catch-up mode," said Porell, noting companies are increasingly looking to retain their most highly valued computing services in-house.

Illustrating this trend, nearly 70 percent of U.S. respondents said they have already or were currently organising their computing strategies around information rather than around technology, as they had in the past.

Noting more than three-quarters of respondents have or are planning to use Internet technology, the survey said there was "a strong indication that IT strategies are increasingly focused on using information to reach business goals."
Unsurprisingly, given increased effort to access and utilize corporate data, respndents also identified information bottlenecks as the next critical problem for managers.

In the U.S., 71 percent said business productivity is hurt by poor performance, and 66 percent said customer service is degraded, while at least 60 percent noted adverse impact on time-to-market and competitiveness.

The survey is based on interviews with information technology executives and managers in 700 organisations, including 300 in the United States, 300 in Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, Netherlands, and Britain -- and 100 in Japan.
